title: The Protégé Effect: Why Teaching Deepens Your Own Learning (2009)
explainer: In a 2009 study, Catherine Chase, Doris Chin, Marily Oppezzo, and Daniel Schwartz had middle-schoolers teach a virtual agent and found they worked harder, monitored their own understanding more closely, and scored higher than students who studied the same material only for themselves, a pattern they named the protégé effect. The mechanism isn't that teaching magically adds information; preparing to explain something exposes the gaps in your own understanding before anyone can even ask a question. That is the research case for why mentoring someone else is one of the most effective ways to solidify what you already half-know.

title: Benjamin Bloom and the Taxonomy of Learning Objectives (1956)
explainer: Benjamin Bloom and a committee of examiners spent years classifying educational goals into levels, from recalling facts up through applying, analyzing, and evaluating, publishing the result in 1956 as a tool for writing better exam questions. The taxonomy gives a mentor a vocabulary for noticing that a learner who can recite a rule but can't yet apply it, or critique someone else's use of it, is at an earlier level, not failing. Structuring feedback and exercises around those levels, rather than just assigning 'more practice,' is a direct descendant of Bloom's framework.
